title: How dental professionals can manage negative self-talk
html:
Rana Al-Falaki explores how negative self-talk can affect dentists’ wellbeing and leadership, and shares practical ways to manage your inner critic.

Every clinician knows the value of a good assistant: someone at your side all day, anticipating, steadying, keeping you on track. Now imagine that same person spent the day muttering that you’re behind, that the patient in the chair is about to complain, that the team doesn’t respect you and probably never will. You’d replace them by lunchtime.

Yet most of us keep exactly that voice on the payroll. It’s the one in our own head.

Self-talk, the running commentary we have with ourselves, is relentless. Research has estimated that we move through more than 6,000 distinct thoughts a day. And the brain doesn’t treat them equally.

Decades of psychology research, summarised in Roy Baumeister’s landmark review ‘Bad is stronger than good’, show that negative information carries more weight, lingers longer and shapes behaviour more powerfully than positive information of the same size.

In dentistry, we are trained to spot what’s wrong – the caries, the open margin, the flaw in a treatment plan, and that negative bias is sharpened every working day.

The problem is that we rarely switch it off when we look at ourselves.

Realising the dream

Dr BK had recently achieved what many associates dream of: buying their own practice.

However, within months, the dream felt more like a weight. The inherited team was polite but distant. Suggestions were nodded through in meetings and quietly ignored. Changes stalled.

Dr BK was working longer days, sleeping badly, getting headaches by mid-afternoon and arriving home with nothing left to give.

When Dr BK joined NAIL-IT in Dentistry’s Titanium mentoring and leadership training programme, they expected to talk about team structures, contracts, perhaps a new practice manager. But within half an hour of our first session, a different pattern emerged – not in what was happening at the practice, but in how Dr BK described it:

  • ‘They’ll never accept me’
  • ‘I should have known better’
  • ‘If this goes wrong, it’s all on me’
  • ‘One bad review and it’s over.’

None of these were facts. They were commentary. But that commentary was running Dr BK’s day.

Five simple ways to make self-talk work for you

  1. Spot the pattern. Notice when you’re catastrophising, taking things personally or expecting perfection. Name the habit before accepting the thought as fact
  2. Check the evidence. Ask: ‘How true is this? What’s another explanation? Would I say this to a colleague?’
  3. Find a useful reframe. Swap ‘It’s all my fault’ for ‘Which part is mine to change?’ Aim for accuracy, not empty positivity
  4. Give yourself clear instructions. Before a difficult conversation, try: ‘Slow down. Listen first. One point at a time’
  5. Coach yourself by name. Create a little distance: ‘[Your name], you’ve handled challenges before. What’s the next step?’

The myth: ‘my inner critic helps me stay sharp’

When we pointed this out, Dr BK pushed back, as many high achievers do. ‘That voice is what got me here. It’s what keeps my standards high. If I go easy on myself, I’ll slip,’ they said.

It’s one of the most common beliefs in our profession: that harshness is the price of excellence, and that self-compassion is a polite word for lowering the bar.

It isn’t true. Harsh self-talk doesn’t sharpen performance; it narrows it. A mind braced for threat has less capacity for problem-solving, creativity and calm decision-making, and instead keeps you in survival mode – running on adrenaline.

It may surprise you that self-talk never stays private. It leaks into tone, body language and the way we brief a dental nurse or open a team meeting. A leader who silently tells themselves ‘they don’t respect me’ walks into the room guarded and defensive, and the team responds in kind.

Dr BK’s inner critic wasn’t protecting their standards. It was quietly creating the very resistance they feared.

The truth: self-talk is a trainable performance tool

Self-talk is a skill that can be trained like any other. Elite sport has known this for years. A meta-analysis of 32 studies found that self-talk interventions produced a reliable improvement in performance, with a considerably stronger effect when people were properly trained in self-talk.

Within NAIL-IT Leadership, self-talk sits in the ‘attitude’ pillar as one of four keys in the Sustainable Success Toolkit, alongside ‘strength’, ‘solution’ and ‘smile’. We worked with Dr BK in the following three stages.

1. Spot the pattern

Negative self-talk tends to fall into recognisable types: filtering out the positives, personalising, catastrophising, blaming, should-culture, magnifying, perfectionism and polarising (all-or-nothing thinking).

Dr BK’s top three were obvious once named:

  • Personalising – every flat response from the team was proof of personal failure
  • Catastrophising – one complaint became the end of the practice
  • Should-culture – ‘I should be able to handle this’ left no room to ask for help.

Naming the type is powerful in itself. It turns what feels like a truth into a recognisable habit.

2. Twist it

Next, we built positive twists – not empty cheerleading, but more accurate and more useful alternatives:

  • ‘It’s all my fault’ became ‘Many things may be responsible – which part is mine to change?’
  • ‘This is a disaster’ became ‘There is a solution to everything’
  • ‘It’s too hard’ became ‘It may be challenging, but I have skills I can draw on.’

3. Use the ‘I AM’ system

Finally, Dr BK learned to use self-talk deliberately, with NAIL-IT’s instruct, analyse, motivate (I AM) self-talk system:

  • Instruct – short, clear cues in the moment. Before a difficult conversation: ‘Slow down. Listen first. One point at a time’
  • Analyse – question the thought before obeying it. How true is this really? What’s the evidence? Would I say this to a colleague? What’s another explanation?
  • Motivate – affirm identity and intent: ‘I am building this team. I am learning to lead.’

One small adaptation made a striking difference. People who coach themselves by name, or as ‘you’ rather than ‘I’, feel less distress and perform better during stressful tasks.

So ‘I can’t handle this’ became ‘BK, you’ve handled harder than this. What’s the next step?’

That small distance created space to think.

Practised consistently, the benefits compound: better mood, focus, motivation and decision-making; lower stress; stronger relationships and team engagement; and better overall performance.

‘Harsh self-talk doesn’t sharpen performance; it narrows it’

The wins

The changes didn’t happen overnight, but within a few months the difference was unmistakable.

At work, Dr BK walked into meetings curious rather than defensive. They stopped pre-empting rejection and started inviting input – and the team began to offer it. Suggestions turned into actions, changes that had stalled for months were finally implemented, and the practice manager described the atmosphere as lighter, clearer and more of a team.

With less time lost to second-guessing and stalled decisions, productivity rose, and revenue followed.

Healthwise, the headaches eased and sleep improved. With energy no longer burned on internal battles, Dr BK found the headspace to revisit the growth plans they had shelved.

At home, the shift was perhaps the most profound. Dr BK was present with their partner and children again.

‘I thought I needed the team to change,’ Dr BK said. ‘It turns out the first voice I needed to stop obeying was my own.’

Choose your voice

You can’t stop thousands of thoughts passing through your mind each day. But you can choose which ones you believe, which ones you challenge, and which ones you turn into instruction, analysis and motivation.

The voice in your head will run your day either way. The only question is whether it’s working for you, or against you.
